Strategy training has been shown to improve performance in working memory, particularly among older adults. However, it does not appear to have a significant impact on age-related deficits associated with working memory.

Research suggests that strategy-specific effects rather than domain-general gains in cognitive ability are responsible for improvements in WM (working memory) performance. This implies that individual differences in strategy use and practice may play a role in determining how effectively individuals can improve their working memory abilities.

While there is some evidence to suggest that older adults with age-related deficits in working memory may benefit from strategy training, the benefits are likely to be modest compared to other interventions. The current literature suggests that strategy-based training programs should not be relied upon as a sole means of improving cognitive function in older adults.

It's essential to note that individual differences and contextual factors, such as the type and duration of training, will also influence the effectiveness of strategy training on working memory in older adults.
